title: Collapse at the GP's clinic after two years of night sweats

source.citation: Mohamed H, Attia AM, John HT, Owies A, Varrier M. Think Addison's Disease: Disseminated Tuberculosis Presenting With Adrenal Crisis in a Young Male Patient. Cureus. 2025;17(10):e94091.

presentation.chiefComplaint: Sudden collapse at his general practitioner's clinic
presentation.hpi: Collapsed suddenly, short of breath, at his general practitioner's clinic and was brought in by ambulance. More than two years of intermittent night sweats, low-grade fevers and fatigue, with over 20 kg of weight loss in the last three months. Admitted with community-acquired pneumonia in March 2024 and again in March 2025, the second time also with persistent anemia treated with iron and vitamin B12 injections. Since then: anorexia, episodic dizziness, an alternately dry and productive cough and drenching night sweats. Yesterday he had two brief blackouts on standing.
pmh: Vitamin B12 deficiency treated with intramuscular injections
Community-acquired pneumonia requiring admission, March 2024 and March 2025
No known HIV or other immunosuppression; no corticosteroid use
presentation.social: Strict vegan, lactose-free diet. Smokes about four cigarettes a day (20 years). Drank 2–3 pints on five days a week until early 2025, now only at weekends.
presentation.family: Father died young of 'bronchopneumonia', possibly undiagnosed tuberculosis; mother treated for pneumonia in 2023.

exam: Drowsy (GCS 13: E3 V4 M6) and cachectic
Diffuse bronzed hyperpigmentation of sun-exposed skin, palmar creases, knuckles and buccal mucosa
Cool extremities with delayed capillary refill; overt circulatory shock
No focal signs of infection; rapid but normal heart sounds; low jugular venous pressure; soft abdomen without organomegaly
Mild generalized muscle weakness; no focal neurological deficit

investigations.name: Sputum mycobacterial testing
investigations.value: Acid-fast smears negative; culture grew Mycobacterium tuberculosis after 1 week

imaging.modality: CT head, chest, abdomen and pelvis
imaging.finding: 2.4 cm spiculated cavitating right upper lobe opacity with extensive peribronchovascular nodularity; bilaterally abnormal adrenal glands consistent with subacute adrenalitis; splenomegaly; thick-walled, peripherally enhancing collection over the left greater trochanter

diagnosis.primary: Adrenal crisis from primary adrenal insufficiency due to tuberculous adrenalitis (disseminated tuberculosis)

management: Treated first as septic shock with broad-spectrum antibiotics and IV fluids; hypotension persisted and needed vasopressors
Hydrocortisone 100 mg IV in the ED, with marked hemodynamic improvement
ICU: hydrocortisone 50 mg IV every 6 h, IV saline and careful correction of the hyponatremia; fludrocortisone 0.1 mg daily added once stable
Antibiotics stopped once bacterial sepsis was excluded; quadruple anti-tuberculous therapy (isoniazid, rifampicin, pyrazinamide, ethambutol) with pyridoxine
Ultrasound-guided drainage of a tuberculous thigh abscess
outcome: Within 48 h blood pressure stabilized, vasopressors were stopped, sodium rose to 128 mmol/L and potassium normalized. Discharged after 26 days on hydrocortisone 20 mg three times daily, fludrocortisone 150 µg daily and anti-tuberculous therapy. At follow-up he was eating better and gaining weight, cough and night sweats had resolved, sputum cultures were negative, and ACTH remained high (persistent primary adrenal insufficiency).
teachingPoints: Adrenal crisis mimics septic shock: suspect it when shock does not respond to fluids and vasopressors, especially with hyponatremia, hyperkalemia or hypoglycemia.
Mucocutaneous hyperpigmentation (palmar creases, buccal mucosa) reflects high ACTH and points to primary adrenal insufficiency.
Give hydrocortisone 100 mg IV at once with isotonic fluid; draw cortisol and ACTH first only if it causes no delay (2016 Endocrine Society guideline).
Tuberculosis remains a leading cause of primary adrenal insufficiency worldwide; enlarged adrenals suggest an infective or infiltrative cause rather than autoimmune adrenalitis.
After glucocorticoid replacement sodium can rise quickly, so monitor it closely; rifampicin speeds cortisol clearance, so replacement doses usually need increasing.

questions.q: What is the most likely cause of his shock?
questions.extra: Na⁺ 106 mmol/L, K⁺ 5.6 mmol/L, glucose 3.1 mmol/L, Hb 82 g/L. Blood pressure stays low after IV fluids, broad-spectrum antibiotics and a vasopressor.
options: Hypovolemic shock from chronic poor intake
Cardiogenic shock from a dilated cardiomyopathy
Adrenal crisis from primary adrenal insufficiency
questions.explanation: Refractory shock with hyponatremia, hyperkalemia, hypoglycemia and mucocutaneous hyperpigmentation is the signature of primary adrenal insufficiency: cortisol and aldosterone are lacking while ACTH is high. Sepsis can coexist and trigger a crisis, but it does not explain the electrolytes, the hypoglycemia or the pigmentation.

questions.q: What is the most appropriate immediate step?
options: Hydrocortisone 100 mg IV now, after drawing cortisol and ACTH
Short Synacthen test first, steroids only if cortisol stays low
Dexamethasone 4 mg IV, so the cortisol assay is not affected
Oral fludrocortisone 0.1 mg and 3% saline for the sodium
questions.explanation: The 2016 Endocrine Society guideline on primary adrenal insufficiency recommends immediate parenteral hydrocortisone 100 mg with isotonic fluid when adrenal crisis is suspected, before test results are available. High-dose hydrocortisone also has mineralocorticoid activity, which dexamethasone lacks; hypertonic saline is the wrong tool for chronic hypovolemic hyponatremia.

questions.q: After hydrocortisone and saline, what is the main risk related to his sodium?
questions.extra: Na⁺ 106 mmol/L; cachectic, with regular alcohol intake.
options: Cerebral edema from a further fall in sodium
Osmotic demyelination from an overly rapid rise in sodium
Seizures from potassium falling with rehydration
questions.explanation: Cortisol replacement and volume repletion remove the stimuli to ADH, so a water diuresis can raise sodium quickly. A sodium of 106 mmol/L with malnutrition and alcohol use means high risk of osmotic demyelination: European (2014) and US expert recommendations cap the rise at about 8–10 mmol/L in 24 h, at the lower end in high-risk patients.

questions.q: Which findings point to a primary (adrenal) rather than a secondary (pituitary) cause?
options: A low random cortisol during shock
questions.explanation: High ACTH in primary adrenal insufficiency stimulates melanocortin receptors and causes pigmentation, and loss of aldosterone causes hyperkalemia. In pituitary disease ACTH is low and the renin–aldosterone axis is intact; hypoglycemia, hyponatremia, hypotension and a low cortisol occur in both.

evidence.quote: A 42-year-old man of Indian origin was brought to the emergency department after suddenly collapsing at his general practitioner's clinic.
Collapsed with dyspnea; brought by ambulance.
The patient's history revealed intermittent night sweats, episodic low-grade fevers, and chronic fatigue for over two years.
He had lost more than 20 kilograms over the past three months alone.
In March 2024, he was hospitalised with community-acquired pneumonia and received intravenous antibiotics without adrenal testing.
he required a second admission for pneumonia, during which persistent anaemia (Hb 70-80 g/L) was treated with ferrous fumarate and intramuscular vitamin B12 injections
he continued to complain of anorexia, episodic dizziness, alternating dry and productive cough, and drenching night sweats
one day before presentation, he experienced two brief blackout episodes at home while standing
His past medical history included iron-deficiency anaemia, strict adherence to a vegan and lactose-free diet, and prior vitamin B12 deficiency requiring intramuscular supplementation.
He had undergone laparoscopic cholecystectomy in 2012 and denied corticosteroid use.
There was no known HIV or other immunosuppressive condition.
Social history revealed a 20-year smoking history (four cigarettes daily) and moderate alcohol intake (2-3 pints on five days a week until early 2025, now weekends only).
his father had died of “bronchopneumonia” at a young age, raising suspicion of undiagnosed TB, while his mother was successfully treated for pneumonia in 2023
he was profoundly hypotensive with a blood pressure of 70/40 mmHg, tachycardic at 110 bpm, and drowsy with a Glasgow Coma Scale score of 13
Glasgow Coma Scale score of 13 (eyes 3, verbal 4, motor 6)
He appeared cachectic, with diffuse bronzed hyperpigmentation involving sun-exposed areas, palmar creases, knuckles, and the buccal mucosa.
His extremities were cool with delayed capillary refill, and he was in overt circulatory shock.
No focal signs of infection were detected, heart sounds were rapid but normal, jugular venous pressure was low, and the abdomen was soft without organomegaly.
Mild generalised muscle weakness was present, though no focal neurological deficits were observed.
severe hyponatremia (106 mmol/L), mild hyperkalemia (5.6 mmol/L), hypoglycemia (3.1 mmol/L), and normocytic anaemia (Hb 82 g/L on admission
Ferritin was elevated at 3102 µg/L, C-reactive protein 67 mg/L, and random cortisol was 102 nmol/L, supporting primary adrenal insufficiency
Arterial blood gases showed compensated metabolic acidosis (pH 7.42, HCO₃⁻ 20 mEq/L
Creatinine (µmol/L) | 102 | 59 | 54
Platelet count (×10⁹/L) | 171 | 216 | 188
Total bilirubin (µmol/L) | 61 | 37 | 24
Although initial sputum smears for acid-fast bacilli were negative, cultures grew M. tuberculosis after one week of incubation.
Autoimmune screening for adrenalitis was negative.
At three-month follow-up, ACTH was elevated with 309pg/mL (reference range: 7.2-63.3 pg/mL), indicating persistent primary adrenal insufficiency
A CT of the head, chest, abdomen, and pelvis revealed a 2.4 cm spiculated cavitating opacity in the right upper lung lobe, extensive peribronchovascular nodularity
bilaterally abnormal adrenal glands consistent with subacute adrenalitis
The CT abdomen also demonstrated splenomegaly
a large, thick-walled low-density and peripherally enhancing collection overlying the left greater trochanter
Cardiogenic and neurogenic causes were excluded by normal echocardiography
Given his refractory hypotension, septic shock was initially suspected and broad-spectrum antibiotics were commenced alongside IV fluids.
Despite this, blood pressure did not respond, necessitating vasopressor support.
An urgent dose of intravenous hydrocortisone (100 mg) was administered in the emergency department, leading to marked hemodynamic improvement.
Over the following 48 hours, blood pressure stabilised, vasopressors were discontinued, serum sodium rose to 128 mmol/L, and potassium normalised to 4.0 mmol/L.
The diagnosis of Addisonian crisis was established, and attention turned to the underlying cause.
a unifying diagnosis of disseminated TB with tuberculous adrenalitis was established
intravenous hydrocortisone (100 mg bolus, then 50 mg every six hours), IV saline for volume resuscitation, and careful correction of hyponatremia
Once stabilised, fludrocortisone (0.1 mg daily) was added to address mineralocorticoid deficiency.
Empirical antibiotics were discontinued when bacterial sepsis was excluded
he was commenced on quadruple anti-tubercular therapy (isoniazid, rifampicin, pyrazinamide, and ethambutol) with pyridoxine supplementation
Ultrasound-guided drainage of the thigh abscess confirmed TB on culture and PCR.
After 26 days in hospital, he was discharged hemodynamically stable with oral hydrocortisone (20 mg three times daily), fludrocortisone (150 µg daily)
he reported improved appetite, energy, weight gain of 2 kg, and complete resolution of cough and night sweats
Sputum cultures converted to negative, consistent with treatment response.
